chunks: I wrote to a man asking him to ask Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him) about the well that is in the house for wudu — drops of urine fall into it, or blood, or something of filth like animal dung and such things fall into it: what purifies it until wudu from it for salat becomes permissible? So he (peace be upon him) wrote in his own handwriting in my letter: 'Remove some buckets from it.'

key_terms.الْبِئْر: Well — a water source dug into the ground; in classical fiqh, wells are subject to specific purity rules distinct from cisterns or flowing water
key_terms.الْوُضُوء: Wudu — ritual ablution performed before salat; the question concerns whether water from a contaminated well may be used
key_terms.تَنْزَح: Tanzah — to draw out, pull up (water from a well); the technical fiqhi term for removing water from a well to purify it
key_terms.دِلَاء: Buckets (dila') — plural of dalu; the ruling prescribes removing an unspecified number of buckets to restore the well's purity
key_terms.وَقَّعَ: Waqqa'a — to sign, write a response, endorse; used specifically for written responses by the Imam, a historically significant detail confirming the authenticity of the ruling

ai.seo_question: How do you purify a well used for wudu that has been contaminated with impurities according to Imam al-Ridha?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazi' sent a letter through an intermediary to Imam al-Ridha (AS) asking about the legal ruling for purifying a household well used for wudu when it had been contaminated by impurities (urine, blood, or animal excrement). The Imam responded in his own handwriting with a terse ruling: drawing out several buckets of water from the well is sufficient to purify it. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that a well of water can be purified by drawing out a specified amount, as the water below replenishes and is considered pure.
